subjects.title: Model selection and gating model changes
learn: Opus, Sonnet and Haiku trade cost, latency and capability; Sonnet is the default start, with moves up or down made only on eval evidence.
A model swap is a release: it needs a curated test set, a grading function and a delta threshold set before the eval runs.
Set the rollback criterion in advance, for example no single document type below 0.85; a stratified eval set can reveal a partial-migration option.
The Opus-everywhere 7x overrun compounded three ways: no tier decision, monthly cost-visibility lag, and no eval set.
Per-step tiering: Haiku for routing, Sonnet for summarization, Opus only where the eval shows it earns its place.

Extended thinking bills thinking tokens as output and adds latency; enable it only for a measured accuracy gap. Adaptive thinking with effort is current; budget_tokens is removed on Sonnet 5 (400 error).
traps: Best-available reflex: choosing the most capable model because the demo must land is an unmeasured choice with a recurring cost.
Threshold after the data: setting the delta or rollback threshold after seeing results is writing acceptance criteria after the build.
Average hides tails: a good overall score can conceal per-document-type failures when the eval set is not stratified.
Thinking cannot hurt: extended thinking adds billed output tokens and latency on every call, so it needs a measured accuracy gap.
One-line swap: a model change looks like configuration but changes product behavior, so it is a release, not a tweak.

questions.stem: A new document-summarization service is being designed and no eval data exists yet. Which model starting point best matches sound practice?
options: Begin on Opus because output quality is the hardest property to recover once users arrive.
Begin on whichever tier the partner demo used, then review the choice each quarter.
Begin on Haiku because cost overruns are the hardest problem to recover once volume grows.
Begin on Sonnet; move up or down only when an eval set shows the need.
questions.explanation: Sonnet is the default starting point; Opus is justified only when evals show Sonnet misses the quality bar, and Haiku only when evals confirm the trade-off is acceptable. Starting on Opus is a reflexive choice with no evidence behind it.
questions.mnemonic: Sonnet first; evals send you up or down.

questions.stem: A stakeholder argues the team should ship on Opus 'to be safe' since nobody has measured Sonnet. What is the strongest architect response?
options: Build an eval set first; move to Opus only if Sonnet misses the quality bar.
Agree, but also enable extended thinking so that quality is fully protected.
Agree, because Opus is the most capable tier and downgrading later is easy enough.
Disagree, and pick Haiku so that cost discipline is enforced from the very start.
questions.explanation: Model moves should be measured, not reflexive. Without an eval set the choice cannot be defended, and downgrading later carries change-management cost.
questions.mnemonic: No eval, no upgrade.

questions.stem: A team is preparing to gate a model swap like a code deployment. Which THREE elements are the minimum they need? Select THREE.
options: A curated test set with known-good outputs covering the real work distribution
A grading function, either model-graded against a rubric or programmatic
A published vendor benchmark score for the candidate model
A delta threshold below which the change does not ship, set in advance
A one-week production canary with no predefined pass mark
questions.explanation: The minimum gate is a representative test set, a grading function and a pre-set delta threshold. Public benchmarks do not reflect your distribution, and a canary with no pass mark is just observation.
questions.mnemonic: Set, Grader, Threshold: three legs of the release stool.

questions.stem: When should the delta threshold for a model-swap eval be decided?
options: After reviewing the first results so it reflects realistic model behavior.
After a pilot with real users, once complaints show what matters most.
Jointly with the vendor once both sets of scores are available.
Before the eval runs, so it is a standard rather than post-hoc acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: A threshold set after the data is writing acceptance criteria after the build. Setting it first means the team does not negotiate with itself when the numbers arrive.
questions.mnemonic: Draw the finish line before the race.

questions.stem: A Sonnet-to-Haiku eval shows 0.94 vs 0.86 overall, with Haiku at 0.71 and 0.74 on two document types. The pre-set rule rejects any type below 0.85. What is the best next move?
options: Accept Haiku because the overall drop is only eight points.
Lower the floor to 0.70 so both types pass and ship fully.
Route those two types to Sonnet via the classifier; send the rest to Haiku.
Reject Haiku entirely and stay on Sonnet for all document types.
questions.explanation: The rollback criterion rejects the full migration, but the stratified results reveal a partial migration: keep Sonnet on the failing types and use Haiku elsewhere, cutting cost without the regression. Moving the floor after the data defeats its purpose.
questions.mnemonic: Floor 0.85 per type; failing types stay on Sonnet.

questions.stem: Why did the document-intelligence team build its 250-document eval set stratified by document type rather than relying on one overall average?
options: Stratification lets the grader be programmatic instead of model-graded.
Per-type scores stay meaningful, exposing weak types and partial-migration options.
Stratification guarantees the overall average clears the threshold.
It reduces the number of documents needed to under fifty in total.
questions.explanation: Variance was concentrated in two document types; an overall average would have hidden them. Stratified sampling keeps per-type scores meaningful so a rollback criterion can be applied per type.
questions.mnemonic: Averages hide; strata reveal.

questions.stem: A launched system runs at seven times its modeled cost with Opus on every call. Which THREE factors compounded to cause this? Select THREE.
options: Caching was enabled on a prefix that was too stable to benefit
No model-tier decision was made, so the most expensive default carried through
Cost was reviewed monthly, so the gap surfaced weeks after launch
Haiku was used on the final response-composition step
No eval set existed to ground a different choice during the build
questions.explanation: The three mechanisms were an implicit tier default, lagging cost visibility, and no eval set. The distractors invent causes: caching a stable prefix is the intended use, and Haiku on composition was not the cause.
questions.mnemonic: Default, Delay, Dataless: the three D's of the overrun.

questions.stem: In the 7x overrun case, what does the lesson 'the absence of a decision is a decision' mean?
options: Postponing model choice until after launch metrics arrive is the safest approach.
Leaving the decision to the vendor transfers the cost risk to the vendor.
Skipping the tier choice quietly defaulted every step to the costliest option.
Not choosing a context strategy defaults to retrieval for most workloads.
questions.explanation: Because the architecture had no tier decision at any step, the implicit default of the best available model persisted into production. Not choosing is not neutral.
questions.mnemonic: No choice still chooses: the pricey one.

questions.stem: After the overrun, which per-step assignment did the retroactive eval support?
options: Opus for routing, Haiku for summarization, Sonnet for final composition
Haiku for routing, Sonnet for mid-pipeline summarization, Opus for final composition
Sonnet for every step, with extended thinking enabled on the classifier
Haiku for every step, with Opus used only as a fallback on errors
questions.explanation: Each step moved down only where its eval showed no regression, and Opus stayed only on the response-composition step where it earned its place. Cost fell 71% and median latency dropped to 940 ms.
questions.mnemonic: Cheap router, middle summarizer, premium finisher.

questions.stem: Which statement about extended thinking is accurate?
options: Thinking tokens are billed at a discounted rate because they are internal.
Thinking is free when only a summary of the reasoning is returned.
Thinking adds latency only; billing covers just the visible answer.
Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and add latency to the call.
questions.explanation: Thinking tokens bill at the model's output rate for the tokens actually consumed, regardless of how short the returned summary is, and generating them adds latency.
questions.mnemonic: Think tokens are output tokens: you pay by the thought.

questions.stem: A team sends a manual budget_tokens thinking configuration to Claude Sonnet 5 and gets an HTTP 400. What is the correct remediation?
options: Raise budget_tokens above the model's minimum threshold.
Move the request to Haiku, which still accepts budget_tokens.
Retry with exponential backoff, since 400s are usually transient.
Switch to adaptive thinking and set the effort parameter instead.
questions.explanation: Manual budget_tokens is deprecated on the 4.6 generation and removed on Sonnet 5, where it errors. Adaptive thinking with effort is the recommended control. A 400 is a request error, not a transient one.
questions.mnemonic: Sonnet 5: effort in, budget_tokens out.

questions.stem: A product lead wants extended thinking on every call 'since it can't hurt'. What is the best architect response?
options: Approve it, since it only improves accuracy and the added cost is negligible at scale.
Approve it on the classifier only, where added latency matters least to users.
Reject it permanently, since extended thinking is unsuitable for production workloads of any kind.
Run evals without it first; enable it only if a measured accuracy gap remains.
questions.explanation: Thinking is a cost and latency tradeoff paid on every call. The case should come from a measured gap, not an assumption.
questions.mnemonic: Prove the gap, then pay for the think.

questions.stem: In the 7x overrun case, where did extended thinking add cost and latency with no benefit?
options: On the routing classifier, which did not need reasoning at all.
On mid-pipeline summarization, which ran on Sonnet.
On the final response-composition step, which needed more reasoning.
On the retrieval step, which ran before any model call.
questions.explanation: Thinking was enabled on a classifier that needed no reasoning, adding measurable cost and latency to every request passing through it.
questions.mnemonic: Router thinking: paying to ponder a sorting hat.

subjects.title: Context window and context strategy
learn: The context window is the model's only active attention space and resets between calls; continuity is application-managed via state, summaries or memory layers.
Retrieval augments the window; persistent state (orders, balances) needs a tool call. Budget for the largest realistic conversation: the window is a ceiling, not a target.
Measure with the usage field and token counting, not fixed characters-per-token ratios.
Monolithic, progressive, retrieval and compaction each earn a place and break down differently; production systems combine them.
Context strategy and context sizing are separate decisions; a 4,000-token prompt can carry 80,000 tokens by turn 30.
Compaction is largely one-way and can drop load-bearing detail such as exact identifiers, numbers and prior decisions.
traps: Memory illusion: the model has no native memory between calls; anything that persists was stored and passed back in by your application.
Fill the window: designing towards the full window means hitting the working-memory cliff in production.
Silent creep: monolithic accumulation across turns inflates cost and latency with no visible signal until billing.
One strategy fits all: no single strategy carries a long-running agent; each handles a different dimension of the problem.
Lossy summary: compaction that drops a once-mentioned identifier or decision cannot be recovered later.

questions.stem: A support chatbot must remember a customer's earlier sessions. Which statement correctly describes where that continuity comes from?
options: The model retains a session history between calls and reloads it automatically.
The context window persists across calls until it is explicitly cleared.
The application stores summaries and passes them back into each new call.
The model retrieves it from weights updated by earlier conversations.
questions.explanation: The model has no native memory between calls. Continuity exists only because the application stored it and supplied it again, which makes it an architectural choice rather than a model capability.
questions.mnemonic: Models forget; your app remembers.

questions.stem: An assistant must report a customer's current order status and account balance. What is the correct design?
options: Embed the records in the system prompt and refresh it nightly.
Expose a tool call that fetches the live records from the system of record.
Rely on the model's memory of earlier conversations about the account.
Index the records in a vector store and retrieve the closest chunk.
questions.explanation: Persistent application state is owned by your system, and the model has no inherent access to it; it needs a tool call. Retrieval and static prompt content risk stale answers for live values.
questions.mnemonic: Live state lives in the app: call the tool.

questions.stem: Why is the context window described as having a 'working-memory cliff'?
options: Quality declines gently and predictably as the window gradually fills with tokens.
Things work until the limit, then fail abruptly; outside the window nothing exists.
Cost drops sharply once the window passes a certain token count threshold.
The window shrinks automatically as the conversation history keeps on growing.
questions.explanation: Inside the window attention is available; outside it the model has no access at all. The edge is hard, so designs that creep towards the limit fail abruptly in production.
questions.mnemonic: Inside: seen. Outside: gone. The edge is a cliff.

questions.stem: How should an architect size the token budget for a multi-turn assistant?
options: Allocate the full window so conversations never need any trimming or summarizing.
Size for the average conversation seen during the pilot phase of the project.
Size for the largest realistic conversation plus retrieval, prompt, scratch and margin.
Size for the system prompt alone, since conversation history is billed separately.
questions.explanation: The window is a ceiling, not a target. Budget for the largest realistic case plus all other context components and margin; designing towards the ceiling means hitting it in production.
questions.mnemonic: Window is a ceiling, never a target.

questions.stem: A team plans to let conversations grow until the window is nearly full because 'we paid for the space'. What is the main flaw?
options: Long windows cannot be combined with a system prompt in the same request.
Nearly full windows disable prompt caching altogether for the whole conversation.
Window space is billed per call regardless of how much of it is used.
It hits the cliff in production, and every token is billed on every call.
questions.explanation: The window limit is a hard edge, and you are billed per token on every API call, so fill-level drives cost and risk. Plan margin below the ceiling.
questions.mnemonic: Aim below the ceiling or crash through it.

questions.stem: How should a team find out how many tokens a request really consumed?
options: Read the actual token counts in the API response usage field.
Use a tokenizer from an older model generation as a close approximation.
Divide the character count by a fixed characters-per-token ratio.
Estimate from the word count of the longest prompt in the test set.
questions.explanation: Characters per token varies by model generation, tokenizer and language. Measured counts in the usage field are what the limit and billing apply to.
questions.mnemonic: Count it, do not guess it: usage field.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices correctly handle token measurement in a production sizing exercise? Select TWO.
options: Treat any fixed characters-per-token ratio as a rough illustration only
Count only the user message, since other content is not billed
Record measured usage and use it for limit and cost planning
Apply the English-text ratio to all languages for consistency
Assume tokenizer behavior is identical across model generations
questions.explanation: System prompt, history, retrieved documents, tool outputs and responses all count as tokens, and ratios vary by model generation, tokenizer and language. Measured counts are authoritative.
questions.mnemonic: Everything enters as tokens; measure, never assume.

questions.stem: In a long-running coding agent, which TWO pairings of phase and strategy match sound design? Select TWO.
options: Session start: a small, stable monolithic prefix suited to prompt caching
Discovery of an unloaded file: compaction of the whole transcript
Context filling after many turns: preload the entire repository
Active work: carry forward only recent state progressively
Session start: retrieve every file the agent might need later
questions.explanation: A small stable prefix at the start suits caching, and active work needs mainly the latest additions. Discovery uses just-in-time retrieval, and filling context calls for compaction, not preloading.
questions.mnemonic: Prefix, recent, fetch, compact: four phases, four tools.

questions.stem: Why can a long-running coding agent not be served by any single context strategy?
options: Only monolithic context supports tool calls and test execution.
Each strategy handles a different dimension, so they work as layers.
Retrieval cannot be combined with compaction in one system.
Progressive context disables the need for any stable prefix.
questions.explanation: Monolithic alone hits the limit, progressive alone cannot surface unloaded code, retrieval alone loses the thread, and compaction alone has nothing to compact until the others build a trajectory.
questions.mnemonic: Four jobs, four strategies, one layered system.

questions.stem: A document pipeline starts conversations with a 4,000-token prompt and sees costs rise with no code changes. By turn 30 the context holds about 80,000 tokens. What is the likely cause?
options: Monolithic accumulation across turns is silently inflating per-call input.
The model tier was changed automatically to a larger one.
Prompt caching is charging a higher write rate on each turn.
Retrieval is returning more chunks as the corpus grows.
questions.explanation: Monolithic context that accumulates turn over turn grows cost and latency linearly, with no visible signal until billing. A progressive or compaction approach limits the carried context.
questions.mnemonic: 4k to 80k by turn 30: the silent creep.

questions.stem: For which TWO situations is retrieval (RAG) the strongest context strategy? Select TWO.
options: Sources that change faster than the prompt is redeployed
Queries that need synthesis across every document at once
A small, fixed policy that every request needs
Knowledge bases too large to fit in context
Tasks whose key detail is split across many chunks
questions.explanation: Retrieval earns its place for large corpora, fast-changing sources, small query slices and citation needs. It breaks down on cross-document synthesis and chunking that splits units, and a small fixed policy fits a stable prefix.
questions.mnemonic: Too big or too fresh: retrieve.

questions.stem: A long-running agent compacts its transcript, and later a decision depends on an exact order number mentioned once early on. What is the most likely issue?
options: The context window has silently reset between the two model calls.
The summary dropped the load-bearing identifier; compaction is largely one-way.
Retrieval scored the identifier chunk too low and missed the top-k.
Extended thinking truncated the earlier turns in the stored transcript.
questions.explanation: Summaries can drop exact identifiers, numeric values, prior decisions and edge cases mentioned once. Because compaction is largely one-way, the original detail is not recoverable from the summary.
questions.mnemonic: Summaries shed detail; the shed detail stays shed.

questions.stem: Which risk is specific to compaction as a context strategy?
options: Chunking splits tables and code blocks across several retrieved results.
Cost and latency scale with every turn of the full transcript.
Prompt caching becomes harder when carried context mutates every turn.
The summarizer is a model call, and its fidelity is hard to measure.
questions.explanation: The summarizer adds latency, cost and failure modes, and measuring summary fidelity against the original transcript is an unsolved evaluation problem. The other options describe retrieval, monolithic and progressive risks.
questions.mnemonic: Summarizer is a model too: fidelity unmeasured.

questions.stem: A design review conflates context strategy with context sizing. Which TWO statements correctly separate them? Select TWO.
options: Choosing retrieval as the strategy fixes how large the token budget should be
Sizing sets how much window to use; strategy sets how context arrives
Large windows make the strategy choice unnecessary for most production workloads
The two decisions interact but do not determine each other
A progressive strategy guarantees the window will not fill during long sessions
questions.explanation: Strategy and sizing are separate decisions that interact; treating them as one is where most context designs go wrong. A big window does not remove the need for strategy.
questions.mnemonic: How context arrives is not how much fits.

questions.stem: A support agent uses a progressive context strategy that carries forward only a rolling summary of recent turns. Engineers investigating a bad answer at turn 14 cannot rebuild what the model actually received. Which known weakness of progressive context is this?
options: Cost and latency scale linearly with total input length on every single turn
The correct source document never enters the top-k retrieved results for the query
The exact input at a given step is no longer reconstructable, which complicates debugging
The output contract stops validating because the summary drops all formatting rules
questions.explanation: In progressive context the carried-forward material changes every turn, so the exact input the model saw at step N cannot be rebuilt, which makes debugging harder. Linear growth in cost and latency is the monolithic failure, and top-k misses belong to retrieval.
questions.mnemonic: Progressive moves on; step N's input is gone.

questions.stem: Which TWO tasks are poor fits for a purely progressive context strategy? Select TWO.
options: An agent loop where each step depends mainly on the most recent state
A review whose verdict needs long-range coherence across the full history
A workflow decomposed into stages with narrow, well-defined handoffs
A decision that hinges on a detail dropped several turns earlier
Multi-turn iterative refinement of a single draft document
questions.explanation: Progressive context fails when a task needs long-range coherence across the whole history, or when a decision depends on detail dropped in an earlier turn. Agent loops driven by recent state, staged workflows and iterative refinement are where progressive context earns its place.
questions.mnemonic: Progressive forgets the far past: long-range or dropped detail breaks it.

questions.stem: A team loads a 150-page contract set into one prompt. Token counts show it fits well inside the context window, so they mark the working-memory risk as closed. What does this overlook?
options: The window limit applies only to output tokens, so inputs are never truncated
Attention quality can degrade on very long contexts well before the hard limit
Monolithic prompts cannot use prompt caching, so the prefix is rewritten each call
Contracts must be chunked into a retrieval index before the model can read them
questions.explanation: Fitting under the hard limit does not guarantee quality, because attention can degrade on very long contexts before the limit is reached. Monolithic prompts with a stable prefix actually benefit from caching, so that distractor reverses the guidance.
questions.mnemonic: Fits in the window is not focused in the window.

subjects.title: System prompts, templates and technique selection
learn: An enterprise system prompt states role and scope, constraints (must and must not), and an output contract naming the response shape.
A template is fixed scaffolding plus parameterized slots, so filling a slot cannot remove a constraint and the safe path is the default.
Description competency: name the scope, the format and the constraints; underspecification makes the model improvise differently each time.
An underspecified guardrail is worse than none because it creates the appearance of a control without the substance.
Technique progression is zero-shot, then few-shot, then chain-of-thought; each step adds tokens and latency, so use the lightest that works.
Prompts do not transfer unchanged across models, so a model swap needs an eval; leading phrasing, unbalanced and stale few-shot examples bias outputs.
traps: Hope as spec: if a requirement is hoped for rather than stated, the model fills the gap differently on each request.
Decorative guardrail: a vague constraint the model can route around looks like a control but is not one.
Heavy by habit: chain-of-thought on a task that does not need it is a recurring token and latency tax.
Prompt portability: a prompt tuned for one model is only a starting point for another; the prompt-model pairing is what ships.
Invisible bias: leading phrasing and one-sided examples bias outputs in aggregate, and stale few-shot examples quietly steer wrongly.

questions.stem: Which structure best describes a system prompt designed for enterprise reuse?
options: A short persona line, with details left to the model's judgment
A long list of examples with no explicit rules
A role and scope statement, constraints, and an output contract
A copy of the user manual, with formatting left optional
questions.explanation: A reusable system prompt states role and scope, the constraints the model must hold, and an output contract naming the response shape. At scale, ambiguity is a defect multiplied across every request.
questions.mnemonic: Role, rules, result shape.

questions.stem: What is the main design goal of a prompt template with fixed scaffolding and parameterized slots?
options: Filling a slot cannot remove a constraint, so the safe path is default.
Every slot can be rewritten by users so that teams keep complete flexibility.
Fixed scaffolding lowers token count enough that caching can be skipped entirely.
Slots let each team replace the output contract to suit local needs.
questions.explanation: The scaffolding carries the consistency and safety guarantees, so users supply variable content and inherit the guardrails without re-authoring them. Templates also concentrate complexity where it can be governed.
questions.mnemonic: Fixed frame, free slots, safe by default.

questions.stem: Applying the Description competency to prompt design, which THREE things should a production prompt name? Select THREE.
options: The scope: what is in and out of bounds
The exact output format or contract
The expected temperature value
The constraints that must never be violated
The name of the model that wrote the prompt
questions.explanation: Description covers scope, format and constraints. That is what separates a prompt that holds in production from one that works in a demo.
questions.mnemonic: Scope, Format, Constraints: describe before you deploy.

questions.stem: A reused prompt says 'summarize the ticket' and the summaries vary in length and structure from call to call. What is the underlying failure?
options: The model has insufficient capability for the task and needs a larger tier.
The prompt is underspecified, so the model fills gaps with different assumptions each time.
The context window is too small to hold the whole ticket text reliably.
Few-shot examples are missing, which always causes variation in output length.
questions.explanation: Where the prompt is silent the model improvises, and improvisation is the non-determinism you do not want in a reused asset. The fix is to state the format, scope and constraints explicitly.
questions.mnemonic: Silence in the prompt becomes guessing in the output.

questions.stem: A reviewer asks, for each requirement the output must meet, whether the prompt states it or merely hopes for it. What is this diagnosis for?
options: Choosing between a prompt library and a Skill for the team
Estimating the token budget for the system prompt and history
Deciding where to place the cache breakpoint in the prompt
Finding underspecification gaps the model will fill differently each time
questions.explanation: Reading a prompt for what it fails to say reveals gaps. The fix is to make the implicit explicit by restating the goal, naming the format and bounding the constraints.
questions.mnemonic: State it or lose it.

questions.stem: A prompt includes the line 'be careful with sensitive data'. Why might this be worse than having no guardrail at all?
options: It looks like a control but has no substance; the model can route around it.
It consumes tokens that would otherwise have been available for prompt caching.
It forces the model into chain-of-thought reasoning on every single call.
It prevents the output contract from being applied to the final response.
questions.explanation: An underspecified guardrail looks like a control and invites false confidence, but a constraint the model can quietly route around is not a constraint. A missing guardrail at least is known to be missing.
questions.mnemonic: Vague guardrail: a lock painted on the door.

questions.stem: Which TWO changes turn a vague guardrail into an enforceable one? Select TWO.
options: Name exactly what must never appear in output, and under what conditions
Add a polite reminder to be careful at the end of the prompt
Place the rule in fixed template scaffolding so slot content cannot remove it
Rely on a larger model to infer the intent of the rule
Repeat the same vague wording in several places
questions.explanation: A guardrail must state its bounds precisely, and living in fixed scaffolding means filling a slot cannot delete it. Politeness, repetition of vague wording, or hoping a larger model infers the intent add no substance.
questions.mnemonic: Name it exactly, nail it in scaffolding.

questions.stem: A team needs to extract structured fields from invoices and a first prompt has not been tried yet. Which approach follows the recommended progression?
options: Start with chain-of-thought, then remove steps that look unnecessary.
Start with ten few-shot examples to anchor the format immediately.
Start zero-shot; add examples only if format or judgment needs showing.
Start with extended thinking and a long system prompt.
questions.explanation: The progression is zero-shot, then few-shot, then chain-of-thought, adding each only if the task needs it. Each step adds tokens and latency, so use the lightest technique that meets the requirement.
questions.mnemonic: Zero, few, chain: climb only when needed.

questions.stem: Why is applying chain-of-thought to a simple classification task a design flaw?
options: It makes the model less accurate on well-specified tasks of every kind.
It is a recurring token and latency tax with no gain.
It prevents the use of a stable cached prefix across requests.
It forces the model tier to be upgraded to the next level.
questions.explanation: Heavier techniques cost tokens and latency on every call. Chain-of-thought suits multi-step reasoning where the path matters, not simple tasks that already work.
questions.mnemonic: Needless reasoning is a tax on every call.

questions.stem: A team swaps a mature prompt from one model generation to a newer tier and finds output quality has shifted. What principle explains this?
options: Prompts are portable, so the difference must be a bug in the new model.
Output quality depends only on the system prompt length.
Newer models always need more examples and more explicit steps.
The prompt-model pairing is what ships, so a swap needs an eval.
questions.explanation: The same prompt does not behave identically across tiers or generations; a prompt tuned for one model is a starting point for another. That is why a model swap is treated as a release gated by an eval.
questions.mnemonic: Prompt plus model is the product.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about prompts across model tiers are accurate? Select TWO.
options: A more capable model may need less scaffolding to reach the same quality
A prompt tuned for one model is guaranteed to work on a cheaper tier
A less capable model may need more examples or explicit steps
Prompts transfer unchanged, so no eval is needed after a swap
Few-shot examples behave identically across all generations
questions.explanation: Scaffolding needs vary with capability: capable models need less, weaker ones more. Because behavior differs, the swap itself must be gated with an evaluation.
questions.mnemonic: Stronger model, lighter scaffolding; weaker, heavier.

questions.stem: A few-shot classifier over-predicts 'approve' in aggregate. Which TWO prompt-construction faults are most likely responsible? Select TWO.
options: Examples that show mostly approvals and few other cases
An output contract that names the response shape
A neutral instruction that lists the possible labels
Leading phrasing that presumes the answer is 'approve'
A system prompt that states the role and scope
questions.explanation: Unbalanced examples and leading phrasing steer the output toward one answer, and bias like this is invisible in any single output, only appearing in aggregate. Neutral phrasing and balanced examples are design requirements.
questions.mnemonic: Lopsided examples, loaded wording, lopsided outputs.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, a few-shot extraction prompt starts mishandling a new document layout even though nothing in the code changed. What is the most likely first thing to review?
options: The retry policy for handling transient API errors under load
The few-shot examples, which may be stale against the evolved task
The cache TTL setting configured on the system prompt prefix
The output token limit set for each individual response
questions.explanation: Few-shot examples are content to maintain; as the task evolves, stale examples quietly steer the model wrong. They should be reviewed and rebalanced like any other asset.
questions.mnemonic: Examples age; stale shots steer wrong.

subjects.title: Prompt caching, modular prompts and Skills
learn: Caching works on a stable prefix: static content first, dynamic content after the cache breakpoint; cache_control markers are explicit.
Cache writes cost more than standard input and reads cost less (10% as an example); the default TTL is 5 minutes, so infrequent calls do not amortize.
Caching is not worth it for small fixed portions or rarely called prompts; model call frequency and prefix size before committing.
What is cached is the prompt prefix, and the response is identical to an uncached call; cached live state creates a consistency window risk.
A prompt library is for one team or codebase with light governance; a Skill (SKILL.md with instructions and scripts) suits repeatable, distributed, governed procedures.
Ungoverned copy-pasted prompts drift into many slightly different versions; versioned reuse with approval and rollback is the control.
traps: Dynamic first: putting per-request content ahead of the fixed instruction block changes the prefix every time, so the cache never hits.
Cache everywhere: caching has a write cost, so rarely called or small prefixes can cost more than they save.
Slow cadence: a request frequency lower than the TTL means no consistent savings, because the cache expires between calls.
Stale cached state: caching content that must reflect live state creates a consistency window that may violate requirements.
Copy-paste reuse: prompts shared by copying drift apart, each with quietly different behavior and no rollback.

questions.stem: On what basis does prompt caching match a request to a stored entry?
options: A stable, identical prefix of the prompt
The semantic similarity of the user message to earlier messages
The model's earlier response to the same question
The hash of the most recent user message only
questions.explanation: Caching preserves the processed prompt prefix so the API does not reprocess those tokens. It matches on a stable prefix, which is why the fixed part must stay genuinely fixed.
questions.mnemonic: Cache the prefix, not the question.

questions.stem: A team put per-request document text at the top of a prompt, ahead of a large fixed instruction block, and saw no caching savings. What is the fix?
options: Shorten the fixed instruction block to reduce write overhead.
Place fixed content first and dynamic content last.
Increase the cache TTL so entries survive longer between calls.
Switch to a smaller model so each cache write costs less.
questions.explanation: Dynamic content first changes the prefix on every request, so the cache never hits. Static content before dynamic, with the breakpoint between them, restores hits.
questions.mnemonic: Static first, dynamic last, or the cache is blind.

questions.stem: An application sends the same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short varying user message. Which optimization most directly reduces both latency and cost?
options: Truncate the policy document to its first 1,000 tokens to cut input size.
Move the policy document into a few-shot example block in the user turn.
Switch to the smallest available model, regardless of how well it fits the task.
Put static prompt and policy before dynamic content, and enable prompt caching.
questions.explanation: A long, stable prefix reused across requests is the ideal caching case. Truncation loses content, and a smaller model regardless of fit risks quality without addressing the repeated prefix.
questions.mnemonic: Long stable prefix up front: cache it.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a cache breakpoint?
options: To mark where the fixed cacheable prefix ends and variable content begins
To split the response into cached and uncached portions after generation
To set the maximum number of cache hits allowed per hour
To flag prompts that should skip the safety guardrails entirely
questions.explanation: A breakpoint marks the boundary between the fixed part of the prompt and the variable part. Caching requires explicit cache_control markers, and the fixed part must remain genuinely fixed.
questions.mnemonic: Breakpoint: where fixed ends and variable begins.

questions.stem: The default cache TTL is 5 minutes. A workload calls the same long prompt once every 20 minutes. What is the likely outcome?
options: Consistent savings, because the prefix is long and stable enough to cache.
No consistent savings, because entries expire between calls and writes repeat.
Savings on output tokens only, since input tokens are reprocessed.
Savings that grow over time because idle periods keep the cache warm.
questions.explanation: Request frequency lower than the TTL means the cache will not give consistent savings, since each call pays the write cost. Match the cache lifetime to call frequency and how often the fixed content changes.
questions.mnemonic: Gap longer than TTL, write forever.

questions.stem: If cache reads cost 10% of the standard input rate and writes cost more than standard input, when does caching produce the largest savings?
options: A short prefix used a handful of times a week
A prefix reused only once after the initial write
A prefix that changes on every request but is very long
A long, stable prefix reused across many requests within the TTL
questions.explanation: Savings scale with both the length of the cached prefix and how often it is reused. The first use pays the higher write cost, which is then amortized across many cheap reads.
questions.mnemonic: Pay once to write, save on every read.

questions.stem: In which TWO situations is enabling prompt caching likely to cost more than it saves? Select TWO.
options: The fixed portion of the prompt is small
The prompt is called constantly with a large fixed prefix
The prompt is called infrequently, so the write is rarely amortized
The fixed instruction block is 8,000 tokens and reused each minute
The static content is placed first and dynamic content last
questions.explanation: Caching has its own write cost, so a small fixed portion or rarely called prompt may never recoup it. Caching is a design decision, not a default to enable everywhere.
questions.mnemonic: Small or seldom: skip the cache.

questions.stem: A stakeholder worries that prompt caching will return stale or altered model answers. Which statement is accurate?
options: Caching stores the final response and replays it for matching requests later.
Caching returns a cheaper, abbreviated answer with the same overall meaning.
Caching stores the prompt prefix; the response matches an uncached call.
Caching changes the response only when the user message is very short.
questions.explanation: What is stored is the processed prompt prefix, not the response. The response is identical to what you would get without caching.
questions.mnemonic: Cache the prompt, not the answer.

questions.stem: A team caches a prefix that includes a live inventory snapshot, and answers sometimes reflect outdated stock levels. What risk was overlooked?
options: The cache write cost exceeded the cost of the original request.
The model rewrote the cached state during generation.
Caching created a consistency window where cached content lags live state.
The breakpoint was placed after the dynamic content.
questions.explanation: If cached content must reflect live state, caching introduces a consistency window that may violate the use case requirements. Live values belong in dynamic content or a tool call.
questions.mnemonic: Cached prefix freezes the facts inside it.

questions.stem: A procedure must run the same way across several products, with versioning, approval and rollback. Which reuse approach best fits?
options: A shared document of prompt tips that teams copy when needed
A Skill, packaged as a versioned self-contained unit
A modular prompt library assembled in each team's own code
A longer system prompt copied into each product
questions.explanation: Lean toward a Skill when the procedure is stable, distributed across teams or products, and needs versioning, approval and rollback. A library suits an often-tweaked prompt within one team or codebase.
questions.mnemonic: Many teams, one governed procedure: Skill.

questions.stem: An engineering team within one codebase assembles and frequently tweaks prompt fragments, with light governance. Which approach is the better fit?
options: A modular prompt library owned by the engineers
A Skill with formal approval workflow for every tweak
A cached monolithic prompt that nobody edits
A copy of the prompt in each service repository
questions.explanation: A modular prompt library is a shared collection of fragments and templates that engineers assemble in their own code. It fits within one codebase and light governance, whereas Skills suit stable, distributed, governed procedures.
questions.mnemonic: One codebase, often tweaked: library.

questions.stem: What does a Skill package together?
options: Only a system prompt and a list of few-shot examples
A SKILL.md with instructions, optional scripts and version management
A cache breakpoint configuration and a TTL
A model selection rule and an eval threshold
questions.explanation: A Skill is a versioned, self-contained unit: SKILL.md packages the instructions, optional executable scripts and version management so the whole procedure travels as one governed artifact.
questions.mnemonic: SKILL.md: instructions, scripts, version, one unit.

questions.stem: A prompt is copy-pasted across five teams, each adjusting it slightly. Which risk does this most directly create?
options: The shared prefix becomes so stable that caching stops working for any team.
The model refuses prompts that appear in several products at once.
Token counts fall below the minimum length that can be cached.
Many slightly different versions drift apart, each with quietly different behavior.
questions.explanation: An ungoverned prompt copied across teams drifts into many versions. Versioned reuse, as a Skill provides, is the control, because a sprawl of copy-pasted prompts cannot be reviewed or rolled back.
questions.mnemonic: Copy, paste, drift apart.

questions.stem: With the default 5-minute TTL, which TWO workloads will realize consistent caching savings? Select TWO.
options: A long stable prefix called several times every minute
A long stable prefix called once every thirty minutes
A long prefix that is rebuilt differently on every call
A long stable prefix called steadily every few seconds
A short fixed block called twice during each working day
questions.explanation: Savings need requests more frequent than the TTL against a prefix that stays fixed. Calls spaced beyond the TTL expire the cache and repeat the write cost, and a prefix that changes each call never hits.
questions.mnemonic: Call faster than five minutes or pay the write again.

questions.stem: Why must a caching cost model include the first request on a new prefix?
options: The first request is always rejected and must be retried at full price.
Cache writes carry a higher per-token cost than standard input on first use.
The first request returns a lower quality answer while the cache warms.
Cached prefixes are billed at the output token rate on every later read.
questions.explanation: Writing to the cache costs more than standard input, while reads are cheaper (10% in the example given). Savings only appear once the write is amortized over enough reads.
questions.mnemonic: Pricey write once, cheap reads after.

questions.stem: Which prompt is the riskiest candidate for caching in its entirety?
options: A prompt whose prefix embeds an hourly-changing price table that answers must always reflect
A prompt whose prefix holds a stable 8,000-token policy document used for all customers
A prompt whose prefix holds fixed role, scope and output-contract instructions only
A prompt whose prefix contains an unchanging style guide reused across all requests
questions.explanation: If cached content must reflect live state, caching creates a consistency window that may violate the use case. Stable policy and instructions are ideal cacheable content; live values belong after the breakpoint or behind a tool call.
questions.mnemonic: Cache the constants, never the changing numbers.
